gaps.sentence: She spent a great ___ of time preparing the report.
gaps.hint: fixed phrase: a great ___ of + uncountable
gaps.explanation: 'A great deal of time' is used with uncountable nouns; 'a great number of' needs a countable plural.

gaps.sentence: I'd like ___ more time to think about your offer.
gaps.explanation: 'A little more time' means a small additional amount; 'time' is uncountable so 'a few' is wrong.

gaps.sentence: She has two children. One lives in Leeds, and ___ lives in York.
gaps.hint: one of a pair of two
gaps.explanation: 'One ... the other ...' is the pattern for exactly two; 'another' would imply more than two.

gaps.sentence: I'd love ___ help with the decorating, if you're free.
gaps.explanation: 'Some' is used in requests and hopes where the speaker wants agreement.

gaps.sentence: She speaks ___ Spanish and Italian fluently.
gaps.explanation: 'Both ... and ...' links two items affirmatively; 'neither/either' pair with 'nor/or'.

gaps.sentence: ___ of my two brothers work in banking.
gaps.explanation: 'Both of my two brothers work ...' is correct; 'all' and 'none' are not used for two.
'Several charges' means more than two; the other options are used only with uncountable nouns.

gaps.sentence: He took ___ notice of the warning and carried on as before.
gaps.explanation: 'Take little notice of' means to pay hardly any attention; 'notice' is uncountable here.
